about: Every algorithm the site runs, once. tools/site/build_pages.py lists them by field on Science (#algorithms) and, in each homepage band's information panel, those with that band in 'bands' (world: the band's drawn world; piece: its live figure; arrival: the transition into it, scrolled or clicked).

algorithms.name: Depth-first maze carving
algorithms.what: A random spanning tree of the screen’s cells: the carver steps to an unvisited neighbour until it is boxed in, then backs up, which makes long winding corridors.
algorithms.where: Clicking into About Me, Résumé or Contact

algorithms.name: Stateless instanced particles
algorithms.what: Thousands of cubes, streamlines, sheets, film strips, sparks and ink strokes, one draw call per kind; each position is a pure function of the scroll, so scrolling back un-builds the scene exactly.

algorithms.name: Greedy list scheduling
algorithms.what: Where and when each of the vortex’s cubes lands: landing slots come in the order the cubes leave, and each goes, through a priority queue, to the cell first in the building order (low and outward first) of those whose paper has already gone. So the bottom corners are built first, then upward and inward, and no cube lands on paper. It is planned once per screen size and handed to the shaders as a small texture.

algorithms.name: Precomputed fields
algorithms.what: The ice’s geometry and padded arrival atlases are prepared in a worker. The vortex schedule, ink reach and click maze are also prepared once and read from textures.

algorithms.name: Dynamic resolution
algorithms.what: A feedback loop on frame time: the renderer steps its detail, then its resolution, down when frames run long (a run of slow frames, or too large a share of them missing their frame over the last second) and back up when they are quick, and hands the pages back to their CSS art if even half resolution is too slow.

algorithms.name: Latest-intent navigation
algorithms.what: Every click or history step is an intent with its own abortable fetch; a newer one cancels the older, so the page you land on is always the last one asked for.

algorithms.name: Painter’s algorithm
algorithms.what: The 48 peaks are drawn tallest first, so nearer, lower ones overlap them as in a real range.
algorithms.where: The 48 skyline, on the homepage and Outdoors

algorithms.name: Legal-move generation and SAN parsing
algorithms.what: Games are read move by move from standard algebraic notation into positions, each move checked against the rules (chess.js).
algorithms.where: The Scotch on the homepage, the replay boards on Chess

algorithms.name: Live data with a saved fallback
algorithms.what: Ratings and games are read live from Chess.com; if that fails, the last good answer saved in this browser is shown, with its date.

algorithms.name: The Burgers vortex
algorithms.what: An exact solution of the Navier–Stokes equations: fluid drawn in toward an axis spins faster as it closes in, keeping its angular momentum, and is stretched along the axis. Scrolled, the vortex stands on the foot of the screen and grows taller; the page is gathered into cubes up the screen behind its top, each height over a long window, so some cubes lag behind. Each cube goes round the vortex one and a half to four and a half times, rising with the wind, and is thrown down and out onto the page it builds. Clicked, the cubes come out of the axis at the link and spiral away to build the page. Every cell sends one cube and receives one.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Science, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Density waves
algorithms.what: The ring’s cubes bunch into five swarms, as stars bunch into a galaxy’s spiral arms: each cube’s angle is drawn toward the nearest crest of a wave that turns with the wind, so the swarms keep turning, even while the page is still, as cubes pass through them.

algorithms.name: Divergence-free vortex field
algorithms.what: Three layers of drifting vortex cells, the curl of a stream function, so whatever follows it swirls without bunching up.
algorithms.where: The ink before Chess and ice dust before Outdoors

algorithms.name: Coloured dew
algorithms.what: Between the cores a fine mist condenses where the nebula is thick, once its gas has cooled, each site after its own random delay drawn from classical nucleation theory, J ∝ exp(−B / ln² S) (on a click, behind a cold front from the click), and grows by a constant condensation flux, as the cube root of time. Every drop holds its gas’s colour. Drops that touch merge, keeping their volume (r³ = r₁³ + r₂³) at the volume-weighted centroid and mixing their colours by volume, a merge snapping shut with a damped wobble (Rayleigh’s l = 2 mode) and, its contact line pinned, never quite relaxing to a circle.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Racing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Every drop a lens
algorithms.what: Each drop is a spherical cap, traced exactly: Snell’s law at the curved surface, then out through the flat pane. A drop looks off its axis toward the far side, so what it shows (the nebula behind it) is inverted and minified, with the focal length of a plano-convex lens, R/(n − 1), each colour bent its own amount. Its colour follows Beer–Lambert’s law through the depth of the cap, T = c^(h/ℓ), so a small drop is pale and a large one deep, its middle deepest. Fresnel reflection (Schlick) shows a dark room and a four-paned window; the stardust it gathered still turns inside it for a while. Artistic: water’s dispersion drawn three times over; on a click, the pane looks onto Racing through a window that widens as the dew ages.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Racing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Supernovae and planetary nebulae
algorithms.what: Science’s sky has a dozen supergiants, each coloured as a black body: Planck’s law integrated against the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions, red at 3,400 K, blue-white at 30,000 K. Moving on to Racing, a few of them end, chosen so that each nebula has room of its own and only the outer fringes of neighbours cross. The hot ones go supernova: each pulses faster and faster, dims as its core collapses, then breaks out in a flash fading along the light curve of nickel-56 decaying to cobalt-56 (mean lives 8.8 and 111.3 days, compressed but in proportion); a light echo races out through the dust, and the gas near it flares in [O III], then glows in Hα as it recombines; the remnant expands freely (R ∝ t), then as a Sedov–Taylor blast wave (R ∝ t^⅖). Each is a different remnant: the Crab (a pulsar flickering in blue-white synchrotron light inside a cage of red and orange filaments), Cassiopeia A (a lop-sided ring of fast knots, oxygen-green on one side and sulphur-red on the other, with a jet), the Veil (braided arcs, each strand red with hydrogen inside and blue-green with oxygen outside, the layering of a cooling shock) and SN 1987A (a tilted ring of hot spots lighting one by one as the ejecta reach it, two fainter rings above and below). The cool giants shed planetary nebulae instead, their cores left as white dwarfs: the Cat’s Eye (nested, tilted bubbles, jets and a halo of rings), the Ring (a torus layered blue-green to red, dark knots on its inner edge) and the Butterfly (two lobes either side of a dusty waist). Artistic: the pace, compressed from millennia to a scroll.
algorithms.where: Science’s sky, and arriving at Racing by scroll

algorithms.name: Gravitational collapse: stardust spiralling in
algorithms.what: Behind each shock the gas breaks into cores, most where its nebula is densest, each the start of a drop. A core falls in on itself as a cloud in free fall: a grain that starts at r₀ is at r = r₀ cos²β when t / t_ff = (β + sin β cos β) / (π/2), at rest at first and ever faster. It keeps its angular momentum, so r² dθ/dt stays constant and θ − θ₀ = Ω tan β: an exact spiral that quickens as it closes. Each grain is drawn as a glint with a trail along its orbit, so every drop gathers a whirlpool of its gas’s colours. The outer shells arrive later, at a steady rate (Shu’s inside-out collapse), so each drop’s volume grows linearly as its grains arrive; the gas streams in too, squeezed brighter as it gathers, and the nebula fades as its gas is taken. The drops’ sizes follow a power law, n(r) ∝ r^−2, a few large and many small. Artistic: liquid water from a nebula’s gas.

algorithms.name: A freezing chain reaction
algorithms.what: A few seeds of ice at the frame’s edges set it off. Each frozen drop grows a bridge of frost across the gap to its neighbours at a steady rate, and a drop freezes when the first bridge reaches it: first-passage percolation over the drops (interdroplet ice bridging, Boreyko & Collier, 2013), so the freeze runs across the pane as a branching tree, flash after flash, the middle last; where the drops are too far apart to bridge, the frost front reaches them across the bare glass. Each drop freezes in two stages: dendritic ice fills it milky in a flash (recalescence), then it clears to a bead of ice in its own colour. Its latent heat evaporates the drops nearby, and the vapour freezes out in a ring, a frost halo (Jung, Tiwari & Poulikakos, 2012). On a click the freeze runs out from the click instead.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Racing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Snow crystals, fissures and the main crack
algorithms.what: As the freeze reaches them, the larger drops (kept a minimum distance apart) seed snow crystals in their own colours, each of its own habit from the Nakaya diagram, mostly stellar and fernlike dendrites, with sectored, broad-branched and stellar plates, the conditions varying smoothly over the pane. Side branches leave each arm at 60° at irregular places and of irregular lengths, nearly but never exactly the same on all six arms, and the longer ones branch again, so no two crystals are alike. Hoarfrost feathers in behind them, frozen drops dim under their plates, and grains of frost glitter. Where two crystals meet the boundary splits, about two in three of them, into a fissure. The main crack is the least-cost path through the Voronoi graph from the left edge to the right, kept near the middle (Dijkstra); the pane comes apart along it (see The rift and the field lines). On a click the cells fall instead, each shrinking into the distance about its centroid, from the click outward. Artistic: the colours the ice takes from the nebulae, the electricity crawling and flickering along the fissures and surging along the main crack, and the shaking.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Racing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: The rift and the field lines
algorithms.what: The main crack opens with the elliptical crack-opening profile of linear elastic fracture (Griffith, Irwin): widest mid-span, closed at its ends. A fracture front runs out from it at a steady speed, and each piece breaks away once the front has run round it, coming apart into fragments. The crack is charged and Racing’s card oppositely, a little more strongly, so every electric field line ends on the card (a two-dimensional Coulomb field, the lines traced with Runge–Kutta). Each fragment, overdamped, moves along the field line through where it was, slowly at first and quicker as the field strengthens, so the pieces are drawn in, vacuumed into the card; each turns to lie along the field (the torque on its induced dipole), spins about it so its face flashes, and fuses into the card where its line ends. The field itself glows as it builds, every line lit behind its fragment, the pattern of a magnet’s filings on a screen. The card frosts from where they land, snow crystals of every habit nucleating and growing into one another, flashes and anneals clear into Racing’s glass card. Artistic: lightning bridging the gap until it snaps, a sunrise behind the ice with god rays and ice dust, the page’s text condensing from frost.

algorithms.name: Thin-film interference
algorithms.what: Light reflected from the top and bottom of a thin layer interferes, so the colour depends on its thickness and the angle you look from.
algorithms.where: The liquid chrome, the ice sheets, and the wing scales on Science (summed with CIE colour matching)

algorithms.name: Fresnel reflection and Blinn–Phong highlights
algorithms.what: Surfaces reflect more at grazing angles; highlights come from the half-vector between the light and the eye.
algorithms.where: The chrome, the ice, the gilt

algorithms.name: Microfacet glitter
algorithms.what: The ice is split into tiny facets, each tilted at random; one flashes only when its own normal lines up with the light.

algorithms.name: Caustics
algorithms.what: Light focused by moving water or rippled ice: an iterated trigonometric warp under the glacier, a drifting Voronoi net beside the peeling sheets.

algorithms.name: Page curl
algorithms.what: Three layers of sheets (the glacier's ice, a topographic trail map, tracing vellum) peel one under another, each sheet from a corner of its own: half a turn round a cylinder, then laid back over itself. Let go, a sheet flies like paper, unrolling, cupping, twisting along its length and fluttering, its normals taken from the bent surface itself.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Outdoors, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Colour negative film
algorithms.what: The page is exposed onto 35 mm film: inverted, under the orange mask colour negatives carry, with sprocket holes along its edges and lines between its frames. Its frames then come up as positive prints in the developer.

algorithms.name: A twisting helix (a framed curve)
algorithms.what: Each strip of film is pulled off the table along a rising helix: its frame (tangent, width, face) is carried along the curve and turned about the tangent, so the ribbon twists as it coils up the screen.

algorithms.name: A blur the vortex sharpens
algorithms.what: The cubes bring Science in heavily blurred, read from a mipmap pyramid of the page (a coarser level the blurrier, in five samples). The vortex’s wide base ring sharpens it: the foot of the screen first, while the vortex stands there, then, once the gathering is done, the whole page from the bottom up as the base lifts and its ring climbs, the blur shrinking continuously under the arch of its tendrils.

algorithms.name: The Lorenz attractor
algorithms.what: Each thrown cube swerves along its own stretch of Lorenz’s chaotic system (σ = 10, ρ = 28, β = 8/3), integrated as it flies and pinned to nothing at its release and its landing, so no two throws curve alike.

algorithms.name: Damped ripples
algorithms.what: Developer ripples spread out from the line where the film lifts, dying away with distance, under the safelight.

algorithms.name: Diffraction spikes
algorithms.what: A nine-bladed aperture spreads a point of light into eighteen spikes, two for each blade edge.

algorithms.name: Kepler’s third law and transit photometry
algorithms.what: TRAPPIST-1’s seven planets at their measured periods; each one crossing the star dims it by the share of its disc it covers, (Rp / R★)².

algorithms.name: Topological flocking
algorithms.what: Each starling aligns with, steers toward and keeps clear of its seven nearest neighbours, however far they are (Ballerini et al. 2008); the murmuration’s shape comes out of that.

algorithms.name: Extrapolating Voyager 1
algorithms.what: Its distance from one reference point and its speed (about 17 km/s), and the light-travel time that distance implies.

algorithms.name: Value noise and fractal Brownian motion
algorithms.what: Hashed lattice noise summed over octaves: the paper’s grain, the nebula, the ink ridges, the developer tray, the fog on history steps.

algorithms.name: Domain warping
algorithms.what: Noise fed into noise, which folds the nebula into filaments.

algorithms.name: Voronoi cells
algorithms.what: Each point belongs to its nearest seeded nucleus. Voronoi patterns shape frost and caustics.

algorithms.name: Recursive branching
algorithms.what: A few trunks that fork three times, each level twice as many branches as the last, wobbled by noise; the ink fills in nearest its branches first.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Chess, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Streamline integration
algorithms.what: Ink strokes traced step by step along the vortex field (Euler integration), tapering as they go.

algorithms.name: Halftone screening
algorithms.what: Tone as dots on a 45° screen, each as large as the tone it stands for; the screen grows finer as the print develops.
algorithms.where: Arriving at Photography: the prints developing, scrolled or clicked

algorithms.name: Ordered dithering
algorithms.what: An 8 × 8 Bayer threshold matrix built by interleaving bits; levels rise from 2 to 32 per channel before the print reaches full tone.

algorithms.name: Time scales and arc length
algorithms.what: The Power Map places 224 moments by date along one line; the Birkie route is drawn to the point the race clock has reached, by arc length along its path.
algorithms.where: The homepage’s About Me band, Racing

algorithms.name: Vogel’s phyllotaxis
algorithms.what: Seed n sits at radius c√n, turned n times the golden angle (137.508°); the seeds pack without gaps in 34 and 55 spirals.

algorithms.name: Barnsley’s fern
algorithms.what: An iterated function system: four affine maps, picked at random, draw a fern made of smaller ferns.

algorithms.name: The Drake equation
algorithms.what: The number of civilisations we could hear from as a product of seven factors, set on log scales where they span orders of magnitude.

algorithms.name: Signed distance fields
algorithms.what: Shapes as distance functions, so their edges stay sharp at any size: the glass card, the iris blades, the maze’s corridors, the crystal on the homepage.

algorithms.name: Metaballs
algorithms.what: The liquid-chrome drops are one implicit surface, the sum of r² / d² from each centre; its gradient gives the normal, so drops merge as they touch.

algorithms.name: Perspective projection and back-face culling
algorithms.what: Cubes and sheets fly toward a camera in front of the screen; faces turned away are skipped instead of sorted.

algorithms.name: Line hatching
algorithms.what: The folio’s copperplate look: parallel lines thicken where the scene is lit, with parametric fern fronds (a curved stem, tapering leaflets) swaying in from the edges.

algorithms.name: An iris aperture
algorithms.what: Nine curved blades as a signed distance field around the click, turning as they close; out-of-focus highlights take the aperture’s nine-sided shape (bokeh).

algorithms.name: A faceted gem
algorithms.what: The homepage crystal: six facets, each a window refracted toward its own corner of a destination’s world, with prism edges and a spectrum cast on the paper.
